overview: The product-design team held its conceptual design meeting for the new remote control to cover trend-watching, component and material options, and the user interface, then settle the concept. Marketing reported that people want a fancy look and feel first, technological innovation second and ease of use third, and that fruit-and-vegetable themes and spongy materials are in fashion. The group settled on kinetic charging with a small watch-type cell (so no docking port), a flip-open design with a black-and-white LCD touch screen on the top half and rubber anti-RSI buttons for the frequently used controls on the bottom half, a plastic case with interchangeable spongy rubber covers in fruit and vegetable colours, and a voice-recognition 'where are you / I'm here' locator if the company's new speech feature turns out to be affordable. The cost of voice recognition is the main open item, with a key-chain style whistle as the fallback; the team breaks and reconvenes in about forty minutes.

topics.title: Opening and minutes of the previous meeting
points: This is the conceptual design meeting, covering properties, materials, user interface and trend-watching; the Project Manager felt the team was slightly ahead of schedule.
Changes from management since last time: teletext cannot be used, the remote is not to be a control for everything, and the company image has to be incorporated.
Earlier decisions: leave out voice recognition, use a flip design, and use a shape different from normal (a shell was one idea).
The Industrial Designer was to look into rechargeable batteries; the team was also to think about a port and an alarm for finding a lost remote.
Target market: young, business people.

topics.title: Marketing trend-watching report
points: Marketing ran its usual market research study with a hundred subjects and consulted fashion and design consultants in Paris and Milan.

The three most wanted qualities are a fancy look and feel, technological innovation, and ease of use; fancy look and feel is twice as important as innovation, which is twice as important as ease of use.
Fruit and vegetables are expected to be the theme for clothes, shoes and furniture, and Marketing asked whether the remote should use it too.
Materials are trending toward a spongy feel, in contrast to last year.

topics.title: Components and power options
points: The Industrial Designer reported that some materials considered last time are not available from stock.
The TA11835 chip is used in nearly every TV remote because it sends standard signals.
No rechargeable battery option is available. Standard AA and AAA batteries were judged too bulky; dynamo (wind-up) charging was judged silly and would need a physical handle, taking more space.

Solar charging was questioned because the team believed artificial light does not count, which would exclude people in basement flats and some parts of the world; most TV is watched at night, though the cell could charge during the day.
Solar cells would have to sit on the case, are large and look identical (like on a calculator), are more expensive than standard batteries, and are not resistant to being dropped or thrown around.
A dual solar-plus-standard-battery setup is possible, but Marketing felt it would detract from the design and add nothing.
The Industrial Designer recommended kinetic charging, as used in wrist watches, charging a small watch-size cell; he has never seen one run out but is not sure how long it lasts.
The Project Manager worried that a remote sits on the side most of the time unlike a watch on a wrist; the Industrial Designer argued the remote draws power only very briefly to send a signal.
The User Interface Designer asked which option lasts longest, since customers should not have to charge a remote daily like a phone.
The Project Manager suggested an attachment so the remote could clip onto clothing and be lost less often; Marketing noted it has not come up in focus groups and suggested setting it aside.

topics.title: Circuit board, standby lighting and case materials
points: Most remotes use a printed circuit board whose contacts close when a rubber button is pressed; the chip turns the button into a code fired out of an LED as on-off bursts.
Circuit boards can be made as large or small as needed, so they can fit the button layout.
To save battery the remote should go into standby when unused; if the buttons are backlit, the lights would switch off after about five to ten seconds of inactivity.
The factory offers plastic (the expected main housing), wood (impractical), titanium (very expensive to process, only a standard box shape) and rubber.
The factory's rubber button material is used in stress balls and is claimed to be anti-RSI, which the Industrial Designer doubted.
Plastic allows curved shapes; the flip design needs two separate hinged units.
The User Interface Designer asked about changeable colour covers; replacement covers would be too expensive in titanium, and Marketing noted titanium marks easily when dropped.

Marketing proposed a plastic base with a removable rubber cover that gives the spongy feel and allows different fascias; the group compared it to grip sleeves on pens and changeable mobile phone covers, and liked that it is cheap and comfortable to hold.

topics.title: Button and touch-screen options
points: Options for the controls: a bare printed circuit board touched directly with a finger, the factory's rubber buttons, or a thin LCD showing an array of touch buttons.
An LCD is flat, so it cannot follow curved shapes, but it would sit flat inside the opened shell; it would be black and white, not full colour.

The Project Manager liked a contrast between a rubber outside and something fancy inside, and asked how users would know where to press on a bare board; the Industrial Designer had not thought about that.

Marketing suggested a small pointer or stylus to help with RSI; the Industrial Designer thought it could get lost, the Project Manager said it would have to be attached, and Marketing noted people could use a pen or pencil.
The User Interface Designer warned that frequent channel surfers would find a pointer irritating and could wear out a touch pad faster than buttons.
With a flip-top the circuit can be split into two boards joined by cabling through the hinge, with standard buttons on one half and more complex controls on the other.

topics.title: Compact-mirror idea
points: Marketing suggested the opened shell could act as a compact mirror that switches to the remote display, like advertising mirrors in nightclubs.
The Project Manager objected that the product is marketed to men as much as women and nobody watching TV wants a mirror; the Industrial Designer was unsure an LCD could give a mirror effect.
Marketing withdrew the idea as a passing thought.

topics.title: User interface presentation
points: Competitor remotes are monotonous rectangular black designs with too many cluttered, repeated and inconsistent buttons; only channel and volume controls are common across them.
Proposed a graphical user interface (icons on the LCD) in the middle of the flip-top, with rubber push buttons for repetitive actions like channel and volume so frequent surfers need no pointer.
The Project Manager asked to put the frequently used buttons on the bottom half, pressed with the thumbs like a mobile phone, with the touch screen above; the User Interface Designer agreed.

A company email says the division has developed a new speech-recognition feature; customers want to be able to find a lost remote, for example asking where it is and hearing it answer or beep. Its financial feasibility needs checking.
The User Interface Designer suggested taking inspiration from vibrant fruit colours such as chilli or tomato red rather than a fruit shape.
The User Interface Designer suggested keeping the standard central volume and channel button pattern that users already know.

topics.title: Concept decisions
points: The team agreed on kinetic charging, which removes the need for a docking port, and favoured voice recognition for finding the remote as a gadget and selling point.
The Industrial Designer noted that if the speech parts are already in stock they will be cheap to manufacture.
The Project Manager said cost is the only pitfall and the LCD is not cheap; a black-and-white LCD like a calculator's is cheaper than full colour.
Marketing asked whether AA or AAA batteries were still needed; the kinetic system uses a smaller watch-type cell.
Agreed layout: LCD touch screen on the top half of the flip, rubber anti-RSI buttons on the bottom half; plastic case with a rubber cover for grip.

Covers will use fruit and vegetable colours, not a fruit shape; the Project Manager said the cheap covers allow almost any look (plain black, glittery pink, zebra stripes, rubber spikes) and the focus is the feel.

Marketing questioned whether the concept is fancy enough for the top market requirement; the Project Manager argued it stands out from beige-and-black remotes, and Marketing agreed it is different enough.
Marketing noted cheap covers let the company respond quickly to next year's design-fair trends.
The User Interface Designer added that the outer casing should be changeable; the Industrial Designer clarified that only the rubber cover changes, not the plastic case.
Marketing recapped the decisions: kinetic charging, watch-type battery, LCD on the top of the flip, rubber buttons on the bottom, fruit and vegetable colours for the rubber cover, plastic case.

topics.title: Locator feature, company logo and close
points: Voice recognition for finding a lost remote is wanted but depends on cost; if it is not financially feasible, a whistle-activated locator like those on key chains is the fallback.
Marketing asked about incorporating the company logo, noting the earlier report said it should be obvious that it is the company's product; the User Interface Designer said it will be in the design.
The Project Manager said the logo will be on it like any product and that advertising will associate the name with the product; he was not worried because the product already stands out.
Marketing asked whether last meeting's beeper locator had been rejected in favour of voice recognition; the answer was that it depends on the expense, and more will be known about cost later.
The meeting ended after an end-of-meeting message; the team expects about forty minutes before reconvening and a questionnaire was mentioned.
